newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers fear being tricked back to jobs.
newsitem.headline: French truckers fear being tricked back to jobs.

text.p: French truck drivers, huddled at barricades on a 10-day-old strike throttling France, welcomed progress towards a deal on Wednesday but said they feared being lured back to work by illusory promises.

At a small rally outside an idled haulage firm at Saint-Pol-sur-Mer, close to the Channel near the Belgian border, truckers said they wanted to avoid the "error" of 1992, the last major truckers' strike.
"Four years ago, we believed the promises," one truck driver from the Force Ouvriere union told the meeting outside the Becquet company specialising in transport of chemicals and oil.
"As soon as we lifted the barricades, the bosses went back on the agreements that had been negotiated," he said. "There's no question of doing the same again."
"We're facing special employers with practices and social relations that date from another age," Louis Viannet, head of the Communist-led CGT union, told the rally of about 30 workers.
In 1992, truckers blocked summer holidaymakers with a 10-day action that led to a so-called "progress contract" in 1994 on shorter hours and better conditions for France's 200,000 truckers.

Yet even the Transport Ministry says just a third of companies fully respect the 1994 pact -- a source of anger for truckers now demanding higher wages, shorter hours and retirement at 55 rather than at 60.

A government mediator at talks in Paris said the two sides had reached agreement on two central demands -- on early retirement and shorter hours -- but truckers are keeping up more than 200 barricades on highways around the country to press for a global accord including wage hikes.
The strike has brought fuel rationing for motorists in some regions, hit supplies of fresh food and forced factory layoffs.
In the Drome region of eastern France, officials said some school buses had stopped running for lack of fuel.

In southwest France, the country's main strawberry producer, Picon SA, estimated it had lost 2.5 million francs ($500,000) since the start of the protests because the fruit could not reach consumers. It planned temporary layoffs.

In western France, wholesale fish markets were either cancelled or hit by falling prices. In Port en Bessin in Normandy, prices were down 30 percent because buyers feared the fish would rot before it got to the shops.
Truckers around France have been camping in their trucks, huddled around fires to keep warm. A main demand is for payment for hours spent waiting for loading and unloading.
At Saint-Pol-sur-Mer, truckers took turns to express their frustrations.
"After an 11-hour-day, a driver was sacked because he refused to get back behind the wheel," said Pierre, a trucker for more than 25 years.
The CGT called a national action day in solidarity with the truckers on Wednesday, but apart from isolated demonstrations, such as by dockers in Marseille, few stoppages were reported.
